column1: Relationship between inflation  unemployment and labor force change rate in the USA

The thesis titled Inflation and Unemployment in Japan: From 1980 to 2050 by Ivan O. Kitov from the Institute for the Geospheres Dynamics  Russian Academy of Sciences  presents a comprehensive analysis of the relationship between inflation  unemployment  and labor force changes in Japan over a 70-year period. The study models inflation (π(t)) and unemployment (UE(t)) as linear functions of the change rate of labor force (dLF/LF)  providing an accurate depiction of Japan's economic trends  including the disinflation of the 1990s and the deflationary period of the 2000s.

The research identifies a statistically significant Phillips curve for Japan  characterized by a negative relationship between inflation and unemployment  indicating that rising unemployment has led to decreasing inflation since 1982. The study also establishes a generalized relationship between inflation  unemployment  and labor force changes  expressed as π(t) = 2.8*dLF(t)/LF(t) + 0.9*UE(t) - 0.0392. This model predicts that Japan will experience negative CPI inflation  ranging from -0.5% to -1% annually over the next 40 years  with unemployment rising from approximately 4.0% in 2010 to 5.3% by 2050.

The introduction of the thesis outlines the research's foundation  which is based on previous studies by Kitov and others  demonstrating a linear and potentially lagged link between labor force  inflation  and unemployment across several countries  including the USA  France  Austria  Germany  and Canada. These studies suggest that the Phillips curves in these countries are not in the standard form but are represented by lagged dependencies between inflation and unemployment. The paper aims to estimate the generalized relationship between labor force changes  inflation  and unemployment in Japan and to explore individual relationships between labor force changes and both inflation and unemployment.

The thesis also addresses the role of central banks and monetary policy in influencing inflation and unemployment. It references studies by Leigh (2004) and Nelson (2006)  which discuss the impact of monetary policy on Japan's liquidity trap and the notion of inflation as a monetary phenomenon. The findings suggest that monetary policy has limited influence on inflation  which is primarily driven by labor force changes and unemployment.

The study further examines the New Keynesian Phillips Curve (NKPC) framework  as explored by De Veirman (2007) and Kamada (2004)  and concludes that deflation in Japan is a natural result of a decreasing labor force rather than an output gap. Other studies  such as those by Sekine (2001) and Feyzioğlu and Willard (2006)  support the thesis's findings by showing that inflation in Japan is not significantly influenced by external factors like foreign countries.

The evolution of unemployment in Japan is also analyzed  with studies by Caporale and Gil-Alana (2006) and Pascalau (2007) highlighting the structuralist approach to unemployment and the long-run equilibrium relationship between unemployment  productivity  and real wages. These findings align with the thesis's framework  which attributes unemployment trends to labor force changes.

Kitov's previous work (2006c) on Japan's inflation model  based on labor force changes  is extended in this thesis to include predictions up to 2050. The study employs a standard best-fit procedure to estimate empirical coefficients  revealing a slope of 1.77 and a constant term of -0.0035 for the relationship between CPI inflation and labor force changes. The thesis concludes with a discussion of the Phillips curve for Japan and the generalized relationship between inflation  unemployment  and labor force changes  providing valuable insights into Japan's long-term economic trajectory.
